title: I have forbidden oppression
hookLine: a sacred hadith: O My servants, I have forbidden oppression for Myself, so don't oppress each other (Nawawi 24, Abu Dharr)
tomorrow: the poor say the rich get all the reward. what's the answer?

lines: I HAVE FORBIDDEN IT FOR MYSELF.
cards: What has God forbidden for Himself, in His own words? Rules usually run one way: someone with power tells someone without it what not to do. The parent who sets a bedtime and stays up all night.
The boss who bans phones and texts through the meeting. Al-Nawawi's twenty-fourth hadith turns that around.

It's a hadith qudsi, a saying the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, relates from Allah, and it opens: O My servants, I have forbidden oppression for Myself, and made it forbidden among you, so don't oppress one another.

teach.b: The word is zulm: wrong, injustice, oppression. The hadith, from Sahih Muslim, goes on, in paraphrase: all of you are astray except whom I guide; hungry except whom I feed.
If the first of you and the last of you, humans and jinn, stood on one plain and each asked, and I gave each one what they asked, it would take nothing from what I have.
Every human, first to last, in one crowd, equally in need. Nobody stands in that crowd as an owner, however much they hold. And here two readings speak.
The first starts with power. Zulm is the strong crushing the weak: the tyrant, the cheat at scale, the system that steals.
If God, who holds all power, forbids it for Himself, those with the most power are the first ones addressed.

teach.h: READING TWO: START AT THE COUNTER.
teach.b: The second starts at the counter. 'Don't oppress one another' is said to everyone, including people with almost no power. So it lives in tip jars and group projects and who gets the last slice.

Big injustice, this side says, is built from small ones nobody bothered to fix. The hadith speaks to both rooms at once. And both readings agree on its ending: it is only your deeds, counted for you, then repaid.
Whoever finds good, let them praise Allah; whoever finds otherwise, let them blame no one but themselves.

how: This hadith qudsi is often recited in full in study circles and khutbahs; Muslims cite it on justice from the personal to the political, and its 'O My servants' refrain is sometimes memorized.

o: anger at someone who wronged you
wronging someone, in big ways or small
a punishment for breaking the law

games.q: the sacred hadith — tap the pairs.
p: the first and last of you

s: the hadith only forbids oppression by rulers
'don't oppress one another' is said to all His servants.
in the hadith, God forbids oppression for Himself
and then makes it forbidden among His servants.
the hadith says people's asking would drain what God has
if every human and jinn asked and received, it would take nothing from what He has.

games.q: you think zulm is mostly about small daily unfairness. your cousin says it's mostly about the powerful. what's her best case?
o: if God, with all power, forbids it for Himself, the powerful are addressed first.
small wrongs don't count; only crimes ever reach the level of zulm.
the hadith never mentions people, so it can't be about everyday life.
games.why: the power reading's best case comes from the hadith's opening: the One with all power forbids it for Himself. the counter reading answers: it's said to everyone.

practice: Bring to mind one small wrong you're part of: a credit you took, a share that's uneven, a reply that's costing someone. Make a plan to right it in one sentence: what, for whom, and by when.
Then let the sit hold the plan, and keep it small enough to actually do.

wordCard.voice: Zulm: oppression, injustice, wronging someone. Forbidden by God for Himself first, then among everyone. Today's word.

carryVoice: In your pocket: no oppression, not in the palace and not at the tip jar. Hadith twenty-four, counted fairly.

sources.ref: al-Nawawi, al-Arba'in, hadith 24; Sahih Muslim 2577 (Abu Dharr), a hadith qudsi
